events.title: A stone London Bridge begins upstream
events.text: Peter de Colechurch began building the first stone London Bridge, a much earlier crossing upstream from the future Tower Bridge site.

events.title: Before the bridge: wharves, stairs and crossings
events.text: The river edge was a working port of wharves and warehouses. Irongate Stairs and nearby river stairs gave access to boats; the Tower Subway and London Bridge were established crossings before this bridge.

events.title: Stage 1: river foundations begin
events.text: Work began in April. Crews built temporary staging and began the piers and abutments; the first iron caisson was sunk in September to enclose work below the riverbed.

events.title: Stage 2: approaches and hydraulic design
events.text: The northern approach and its chain anchorage entered construction, followed by hydraulic machinery contracts. Foundation work continued in the river.

events.title: Stage 3: southern approach
events.text: The southern approach and its chain anchorage entered construction. Design work continued while crews advanced the foundations and shore structures.

events.title: Stage 4: steel and masonry superstructure
events.text: Contracts began for the iron and steel superstructure and the masonry superstructure. The contemporary contract schedule dates both awards to May.

events.title: Stage 5: foundation works and rising steelwork
events.text: Foundation and tower construction advanced from the caisson works toward the visible steel towers. The precise sequence of work during this year is not itemised in the cited contract table.
events.note: Year-specific visual state is an interpolation between the dated foundation contracts and the circa-1891 archive photograph.

events.title: Stage 6: tower frames rise
events.text: An archive photograph records both steel tower frames under construction, with the north tower further advanced and a temporary shore span carrying materials.

events.title: Stage 7: high-level walkways approach completion
events.text: The high-level walkways approached completion and the masonry work continued. Paving and lighting entered the contract programme.

events.title: Stage 8: bascule girders and finishing work
events.text: Photographs show the north bascule's four main girders and cross-bracing. Work continued toward completion of the bridge and its machinery.

events.title: Stage 9: tested and opened
events.text: The final granite stone was set in January; engineers tested the hydraulics in April. The Prince of Wales opened the bridge on 30 June.

events.title: High-level walkways close
events.text: Low use led to the closure of the elevated pedestrian routes. Many pedestrians preferred waiting at road level for the leaves to close.

events.title: Electric power replaces steam
events.text: Electric operation took over from the original steam-powered hydraulic system. The historic steam engines remain in the engine rooms.

events.title: Walkways reopen as a visitor attraction
events.text: The public could again enter the high-level walkways as part of the new visitor attraction.

facts.text: The central bascule opening is reported as 200 feet (60.96 metres) clear.
Each suspension side span is 270 feet (82.296 metres) long.
The contemporary account records about 31 million bricks and 14,000 tons of iron and steel used in construction.
The walkways allowed pedestrians to cross above the roadway while the bascules were raised; they closed to the public in 1910 and reopened in 1982.
Steam-powered bridge lifting was replaced by electric operation in 1976.

facts.title: Original water-hydraulic lift cycle
facts.text: The Victorian steam engines pumped recirculated water into weighted accumulators; released pressurised water drove hydraulic engines, pinions and quadrant racks to move each bascule. Today electric pumps power an oil-hydraulic system.

facts.title: Original accumulator pressure
facts.text: The two south-approach accumulators each had a 20-inch ram and worked at 700–800 pounds per square inch. Two additional 22-inch ram accumulators were installed at each pier.

facts.title: Original pumping plant
facts.text: The pumping plant had two steam engines. Each had four steam cylinders and two hydraulic pumps; the engines ran at 45 revolutions per minute.

facts.title: Original hydraulic drive engines
facts.text: Each pier had four hydraulic engines, with three cylinders and a 12-inch stroke per engine. One engine could open a bascule in calm conditions; two could work together against greater wind pressure.

facts.title: River-pier caisson layout
facts.text: Each pier foundation used eight square caissons measuring 28 feet on each side, plus four triangular cutwater caissons.

facts.title: Construction time
facts.text: Tower Bridge took eight years to build from the start of construction to completion.
facts.locator: Official construction timeline, 1886 construction begins; ‘Did you know’ duration statement.

facts.title: Rivets used in construction
facts.text: More than 13 million rivets were used to assemble the steelwork of Tower Bridge.
facts.locator: Official top facts, ‘It took immense skill to build.’

facts.title: Horses and period road traffic
facts.text: When Tower Bridge opened in 1894, an estimated 8,000 horse-drawn vehicles crossed it each day.
facts.locator: Timeline, 29 July 1894: estimated daily road and pedestrian traffic.

facts.title: Why Tower Bridge had horses
facts.text: Horses were part of Tower Bridge's own operation when it opened: horses stabled beneath the southern approach could help carts struggling up the bridge incline. The site also records a blacksmith caring for horses and repairing bridge equipment.

facts.title: The first ship through Tower Bridge
facts.text: The first vessel through Tower Bridge at its opening was the Harbour Master’s cutter Daisy.

facts.title: The sailing barque in the river scene
facts.text: The early river scene uses a generic three-masted sailing barque to evoke the cargo ships that needed access to the Pool of London. It is an illustrative reconstruction, not a specific documented vessel or passage.
facts.method: The scene's ship mesh is a representative barque; the cited history supports sailing cargo ships in the period but does not identify this model.

facts.title: Tug, coaster and Clipper models in later views
facts.text: Later river views use representative tug-and-lighter, motor-coaster and Clipper-style models. These show changing kinds of river traffic; they are not claims that a particular named vessel passed Tower Bridge in the displayed year.
facts.method: The displayed classes follow the scene's era model; archival records document Tower Bridge tug Naja, and the Clipper operator documents its passenger-catamaran service. The individual rendered models are illustrative.

facts.title: How do the bascules open?
facts.text: In 1894, steam engines pumped water into accumulators, which stored pressure until a lift was needed. Releasing that pressurised water drove hydraulic engines and gears that raised the bascules. Today electric pumps drive an oil-hydraulic system.

facts.title: Why are there horses on the bridge?
facts.text: The horse-drawn carts and cabs represent the bridge's early road traffic. When Tower Bridge opened in 1894, horse-drawn vehicles crossed it every day alongside pedestrians.

facts.title: Construction cranes and temporary working platforms
facts.text: During construction, temporary platforms and pile staging gave workers access to the river piers. Cranes lifted excavated material for removal by barges and helped place bridge components. The exact layout of the rendered equipment is illustrative.
facts.locator: Official timeline; Tuit's contemporary account of foundations and construction.

facts.title: What powered it in 1894?
facts.text: The engine house held the steam-powered pumps that supplied the bridge's original hydraulic machinery. The pumps pressurised water; accumulators stored it so the bridge could draw power when a bascule lift was required.

facts.title: What were the stairs and lifts for?
facts.text: The stairs and hydraulic lifts carried people between the road level and the high-level walkways. The walkways gave pedestrians a way across the river while the bascules were raised for ships.

facts.title: Why do the traffic gates close?
facts.text: The gates stop road users entering the bascules when a bridge lift is under way. The road must be clear before the leaves rise for a vessel, and traffic waits until the bridge is ready to use again.

facts.title: Why does the bridge lift for ships?
facts.text: Tower Bridge was designed to carry road traffic across the Thames while allowing river vessels to pass through the central opening. At the 1894 opening ceremony, the first vessel through was the Harbour Master's cutter Daisy.

facts.title: Why do pipes cross the high-level walkway?
facts.text: In the original water-hydraulic system, pressure pipes carried water from the pumping plant on the south side, up the south tower, across the high-level crossing and down to machinery at the north pier. Return pipes brought water back to the pumps, completing the circuit.
facts.locator: Barry's 1894 lecture and Tuit's 1894 account of the hydraulic machinery.

facts.title: Temporary staging across the river works
facts.text: The timber platform and jetty represent temporary pile staging used to reach and build the river piers. John Wolfe Barry describes pilework in the river supporting temporary bridges between shore and pier; Parliament required a navigable channel to remain open during construction. The scene's exact footprint and placement are illustrative, not a surveyed reconstruction.
facts.method: The primary account confirms pile staging and temporary bridges; the scene geometry and precise arrangement are reconstructed.

facts.title: Iron caissons inside temporary river works
facts.text: The scene's timber ring is a simplified visual cue for temporary foundation works, not the actual material of the pier caissons. Barry describes wrought-iron caissons sunk into the riverbed; their upper temporary sections excluded water while the pier masonry was built, and could later be removed. The rendered cofferdam shape should not be read as a measured historical plan.
facts.method: The source documents iron caissons and temporary water-excluding sections; the scene simplifies these distinct works into one timber-colored enclosure.

facts.title: Pile-driving rig
facts.text: Piles supported the temporary staging around the piers. This steam-powered leader and drop-hammer assembly illustrates how pile-driving work could be carried out; the 1894 descriptions confirm pilework but do not identify this exact rig or its position at Tower Bridge.
facts.method: The account documents piles and pile staging, not the rendered machine's configuration; its form and location are an explanatory reconstruction.

facts.title: Cranes, barges and river deliveries
facts.text: Barry records cranes lifting excavated material from the caissons for removal by barge. He also describes cranes moving along temporary timber bridges to place chain sections on trestles. The scene's moored lighters represent riverborne work and supply; their count, dimensions and exact mooring positions are illustrative.
facts.method: Cranes, barges and temporary bridges are documented; the specific vessels and their placement in the 3D scene are not individually identified by the sources.

facts.title: Illustrative derrick on the rising frame
facts.text: This timber derrick shows a possible lifting arrangement as the tower frame rises. Barry's account documents cranes on temporary stages and the sequence of erecting steelwork, but does not confirm a derrick of this design or its placement on top of a tower. Treat this mesh as a visual explanation of lifting work, not a documented Tower Bridge machine.
facts.method: The frame's growth is documented in the account and archive photograph; this derrick's form and location are an artist's reconstruction.

facts.title: Scaffolds and trestles for the high-level chains
facts.text: Barry describes scaffolds and trestles resting on the temporary bridge to erect the suspension chains. He also says the high-level walkways were assembled outward from the tower tops without scaffolding below them. The wraparound scaffold shown on the tower is therefore an illustrative access structure, not a claim that this exact scaffold was documented there.
facts.method: The source documents chain scaffolds and trestles, while the scene's tower-wrapping scaffold is inferred and should not be mistaken for evidence of its exact historical form.

facts.title: Road traffic stops before a bridge lift
facts.text: Before a lift, road traffic had to stop and the bridge had to clear. Barry describes interlocked controls in cabins on the piers, compared with a railway signal box. The scene's swinging boom barriers and their automatic red/green behavior make that safety sequence visible; the sources cited here do not establish this exact barrier design as the 1894 installation.
facts.method: Stopping and clearing road traffic and interlocked controls are documented; the rendered boom barriers and their modern-looking lamps are explanatory scene elements.

facts.title: Signals tell vessels whether the bridge is open
facts.text: In his 1894 description, Barry specifies semaphore signals by day and signal lamps at night to show river vessels whether the bridge was open or shut. He describes green lamps for an open bridge and red lamps for a closed one, interlocked with the machinery so an incorrect indication could not be shown. This is the documented river-traffic signal system, separate from the scene's road barriers.

facts.title: Which ship is visible in each era?
facts.text: The river scene changes from a sailing barque to a steam tug with a lighter, then a motor coaster and a Clipper-style passenger catamaran. These are representative reconstructions rather than verified named ships in a historical photograph. Their rendered sizes and passage timings are inferred.
